title: Number Talks & Number Strings
subtitle: A short, daily mental-math discussion where students build and defend strategies out loud — one rich problem, or a sequenced string of them. The anchor routine for fluency from understanding.

sections.label: What it is
sections.sources: Sources: Parrish, Number Talks (2010) · Fosnot & Dolk / Pamela Harris (number strings) · NCTM, Principles to Actions (2014) · Adding It Up (2001) · Bay-Williams & SanGiovanni, Figuring Out Fluency (2021).

blocks.text: A Number Talk is a brief, daily routine in which the teacher poses one carefully chosen problem, students solve it *mentally*, and then the class shares and discusses the different strategies they used.

There is no paper-and-pencil computation and no rush for speed. The goal is not the answer — it is the **thinking**. Students reason about numbers and operations, listen to one another, and discover that there are many valid, efficient ways to think. Over time, students build flexible, accurate, and efficient strategies: real **procedural fluency that grows out of understanding**, not memorized rules.

Number Talks are our anchor opener because they are the lowest-lift, highest-leverage way to shift from “procedural-heavy, low discourse” to a classroom where students reason and talk. They fit *inside* the lessons teachers already run — no full redesign required — and they build the rational-number fluency our students most need.
Two flavors: a single problem or a string
A Number Talk can take either shape — same routine, same talk moves, same 10–15 minutes:

items: **A single problem** — one rich computation (e.g., `3/4 + 5/6`) with many strategies surfaced and compared.

**A Number String** — a short, sequenced set of related problems posed one at a time, where each “helper” gives a foothold for the next, nudging students toward a target strategy (e.g., `1/2 + 1/2 → 1/2 + 1/4 → 3/4 + 1/4 → 3/4 + 5/6`, building “make a whole”).

blocks.text: Reach for a **single problem** to surface and compare many strategies; reach for a **string** when you want the sequence to lead students to one specific strategy. The Lesson Design section has a bank of ready strings.
What it develops
A single well-run Number Talk touches most of our two frameworks at once:

blocks.label: Strands of Mathematical Proficiency
items: Conceptual understanding
Procedural fluency
Adaptive reasoning
Productive disposition

blocks.label: Effective Teaching Practices
items: Pose purposeful questions
Facilitate meaningful discourse
Build fluency from understanding
Elicit & use evidence of thinking
Use & connect representations

blocks.text: The structure of a Number Talk

items: **Pose the problem.** Display one problem chosen to surface a target strategy (e.g., `3/4 + 5/6`). Keep it visible.

**Silent think time.** Students solve mentally. They show a quiet thumbs-up against their chest when they have an answer — and a second finger for a second strategy. No hands waving; this protects thinkers who need more time.
**Collect answers.** Record *all* answers offered — right and wrong — without judgment: “I have 19/12, 1 and 7/12, and 8/10. Any others?”
**Students share strategies.** Ask “How did you get that? Convince us.” The student explains; the teacher **records the thinking** publicly so everyone can see it.
**Connect & compare.** “How is Maria’s strategy like Devon’s? Which is more efficient here? When would you use each?” Name the mathematics.

blocks.text: That is the whole routine — 10 to 15 minutes, most days, before the main lesson.
What it looks and sounds like

yes.title: We want to see & hear
items: Students explaining *why*, not just stating answers
Multiple strategies recorded publicly for one problem
“I respectfully disagree because…” / “I can add on…”
The teacher recording student thinking faithfully
Wrong answers treated as worth discussing
Wait time — comfortable silence while students think

no.title: We should not see
items: A race to the fastest correct answer
The teacher showing “the” strategy and moving on
The same three hands answering every time
Students working it out on paper
“Good job, that’s right” ending the thinking early
Timed drills or flash-card speed pressure

blocks.title: What a Number Talk is NOT

blocks.text: It is **not** a timed fluency drill, a warm-up worksheet, or a guess-what-the-teacher-is-thinking game. If students are racing the clock or hunting for one “right” method, it has become the very thing we are trying to move away from. Speed is a by-product of understanding, never the goal.
Number Talks are one of the most equitable routines in mathematics — *when run intentionally*:

items: **Multilingual learners:** the silent think time plus a turn-and-talk before whole-group sharing lets students rehearse language first. Provide a strategy/sentence stem bank (“I started by…”, “I changed ___ into ___ because…”).
**Students with IEPs/504s:** no reading load and no timed pressure lowers the barrier; mental math with public recording supports working-memory needs.

**Status & participation:** recording *every* strategy by name (“Jordan’s strategy”) publicly values diverse thinking and disrupts the “only fast kids are good at math” story — directly building productive disposition.

**Culturally responsive:** honoring the many ways students were taught to compute (including methods from home or prior countries) affirms students’ mathematical identities and expands the whole class’s strategy repertoire.

blocks.text: Start with whole-number and friendly problems for the first two weeks to teach the *routine* (signals, recording, talk moves) before the rational-number content gets hard. Establish the norm: **mistakes are how we learn here.**

blocks.text: A Number Talk is **one Opener routine** — one of several you choose from based on the day’s purpose. It is the routine we anchor on as we build out our openers.

The Opener is a **fluid slot**, not a fixed step. Some days you build fluency from understanding (a Number Talk, Quick Images, Same But Different); some days you spiral prior learning or spark estimation; some days you launch straight into a task. Reach for a Number Talk when your purpose is **building flexible strategies and number sense through discussion**.

blocks.title: When to reach for this opener (vs. another)

blocks.text: Choose a **Number Talk** when you want students to build and compare mental strategies for a single idea. Choose [**Spiral / Retrieval Review**](/math/approach/spiral-review) when the purpose is to revisit older content; [**Number Strings**](/math/approach/number-strings) when you want a tighter sequence driving toward one target strategy; [**Would You Rather / Estimation**](/math/approach/would-you-rather) when you want a low-floor reasoning hook.

Whatever you choose, the Opener does **not** replace your core curriculum lesson — it primes it. Because a Number Talk and the day’s lesson can share a mathematical theme (e.g., a fraction-addition Number Talk before a proportional-reasoning lesson), the routine warms up exactly the thinking students will need minutes later.

Run regularly, a Number Talk does four things at once: students reason and talk every day, multiple strategies get surfaced and recorded, rational-number fluency grows out of understanding, and — because every strategy is celebrated by name — students come to see themselves as capable mathematical thinkers.
Planning a Number Talk in ten minutes

The teacher’s prep is short but it is the part that makes or breaks the routine. This is also the seed of the “Anticipate” move from the [5 Practices](/math/approach/five-practices), a Core Instruction strategy.

items: **Name the goal.** What one idea or strategy do you want to surface today? (e.g., “use a benchmark of 1 to add fractions.”)
**Choose & sequence the problem(s).** Pick a problem — or a short string of 2–4 related problems — that builds toward the goal (see the bank below).
**Anticipate strategies.** Jot the 3–4 ways students might solve it, including a likely *wrong* one. Now you will recognize thinking when you hear it.
**Plan your recording.** Decide how you will represent each strategy (number line, equation, area model) so the math stays visible.
**Pick one talk move to lean on.** Revoicing? “Who can add on?” Turn-and-talk? One is plenty while the routine is new.

blocks.text: A bank of rational-number strings (6–8)

Each row is a short **number string** — a sequenced talk. Pose the problems one at a time; earlier “helper” problems give students a foothold for the target problem. (For a single-problem talk, just use the last problem in a row on its own.)

rows: Use “make a whole” and benchmarks instead of jumping straight to a common denominator.
Build 15% from 10% + 5%; transfer the chunking strategy to a new whole.
Reason with distance/direction on a number line; connect subtraction to adding the opposite.
Which is greater: `0.4` or `3/8`? Then `2/3` or `5/8`?
Compare to benchmarks (1/2) rather than converting everything to decimals.
Halving/doubling and finding a unit rate as a reusable tool — the heart of 6–8 math.
See “of” as scaling; connect the fraction and decimal forms of the same quantity.

blocks.text: A sustainable weekly rhythm

**2–3 Number Talks per week** is a sustainable target — enough to build the habit without overloading teachers learning a new routine. Anchor them to the same days (e.g., Mon/Wed/Fri) so the routine becomes automatic for students and teachers alike.
The teacher’s role — and what to let go of

yes.title: The teacher does
items: Pose, then protect silent think time
Record student thinking faithfully and publicly
Ask “how” and “why,” then step back
Connect and name strategies at the end
Welcome and probe wrong answers

no.title: The teacher lets go of
items: Being the source of the one right method
Correcting in the moment (let the class reason)
Rushing to the answer
Calling only on quick hands
Turning it into graded practice
**Build in a turn-and-talk** before whole-group sharing so every student — especially multilingual learners — rehearses their idea with a partner first.
**Post sentence stems** and keep a visible strategy wall so language and methods are supported, not assumed.
**Vary who shares.** Recording strategies by student name and deliberately sequencing from accessible to sophisticated lets more students see their thinking valued.
**Choose numbers that invite multiple paths** so there is a genuine entry point for every student, which is the most powerful access move of all.

blocks.text: Where this leads

The discourse habits students and teachers build in Number Talks — sharing strategies, justifying reasoning, recording thinking publicly — are exactly the muscles needed for [**Core Instruction**](/math/approach/rich-tasks), when we move into full tasks (“task before tell”), monitoring student work, and consolidating with the [5 Practices](/math/approach/five-practices). Number Talks are not a detour from that work; they are the on-ramp to it.
